title: The Highway of Tears (And Maybe Hope)
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the Highway of Tears, the stretch of Highway 16 in British Columbia between Prince Rupert and Prince George where many women, mostly Indigenous, have been murdered or disappeared, many of them hitchhiking. They trace the first known murder in 1969, the 1981 RCMP cooperation, the families' memorial walks and the term coined by Florence Nezil, the 2002 disappearance of Nicole Hoar and the "missing white woman syndrome," Project E-Panana and its three criteria, the victims added to the list, the Bobby Jack Fowler and Gary Taylor Handlin cases, Cody Legebokoff, the 2006 awareness walk and symposium, police distrust and abuse, the 2015 email deletion finding and RCMP apology, missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls, man camps and resource extraction, transit and cell coverage efforts, and the 2023-era shift to hopeful billboards and a proposed rename. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about mushroom supplements.
topics: missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as a grim topic and set up the Highway of Tears.

segments.title: Overview of Highway 16 and the murders
segments.summary: Highway 16 runs about 720 km from Prince Rupert to Prince George in British Columbia, a remote road where many mostly Indigenous women were picked up and murdered or disappeared. Sources include Al Jazeera's 2021 series. The hosts note the national attention the case has received.

segments.title: Earliest murders and early police cooperation
segments.summary: The first murder in the canon was Gloria Moody in 1969. By 1981 RCMP detectives from across British Columbia and Alberta met to compare unsolved cases.

segments.title: Ramona Wilson and family-led organizing
segments.summary: Ramona Wilson disappeared in June 1994 at sixteen; her body was found about ten months later. Her family and community organized searches and started an annual memorial walk in 1995. Florence Nezil coined the term Highway of Tears at a 1998 vigil and later started a full-length walk.

segments.title: Nicole Hoar and missing white woman syndrome
segments.summary: Nicole Hoar's 2002 disappearance drew national attention. Gwynne Dyer's term 'missing white woman syndrome' describes how media and police respond more to white victims. The hosts discuss the bittersweet effect of her case.

segments.title: Project E-Panana and its criteria
segments.summary: In 2005 the RCMP launched the Unsolved Homicide Unit and Project E-Panana, suspecting a serial killer. Three criteria were used: female, last seen within a mile of Highway 16, and involved in high-risk activities such as sex work or hitchhiking. Roxanne Thiara, Ramona Wilson and Alicia Germaine were early cases.

segments.title: Additional victims on the list
segments.summary: Victims added after the criteria include Alberta Williams, Delphine Nikal, Lana Derrick, Tamara Chipman, and Aielle Sarah Auger, the last officially added in 2006.

segments.title: Backlog of boxes and the 1969-1981 cases
segments.summary: Police found about 300 boxes of files, logged them into a database over about a year, and added older cases from 1969 to 1981, including Monica Jack, Micheline Pare, Gail Weiss, Pamela Darlington, Colleen MacMillan, Monica Ingus and Maureen Mosie. Advocates believe the true total could be near fifty.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Break for sponsor messages.

segments.title: Bobby Jack Fowler and Colleen MacMillan case
segments.summary: DNA matching linked Colleen MacMillan's 1974 murder to American Bobby Jack Fowler, who died in prison in 2006. He was also suspected in Pamela Darlington and Gail Weiss murders from 1973, and up to about twenty murders are attributed to him.

segments.title: Gary Taylor Handlin conviction
segments.summary: Gary Taylor Handlin is the only living person convicted in one of these murders, the 2019 conviction for the 1980s killing of twelve-year-old Monica Jack. He confessed during a Mister Big sting operation; the confession about Katherine Mary Herbert was ruled admissible.

segments.title: Cody Legebokoff and later murders
segments.summary: Cody Legebokoff killed three women and a fifteen-year-old girl from Prince George between 2009 and 2010, was caught after a speeding stop, and was sentenced to 25 years, with parole possible after 15.

segments.title: 2006 awareness walk and symposium
segments.summary: In 2006 Florence Nezil organized a two-week Highway of Tears Awareness Walk ending at a symposium in Prince George with about 500 delegates, which produced recommendations. Brenda Wilson works for Carrier Sekani Family Services, often unpaid due to funding shortages.

segments.title: Police distrust, abuse and record handling
segments.summary: Gladys Radek, an aunt of Tamara Chipman, leads Tears for Justice and distrusts police after RCMP officers assaulted her as a teen. A 2012 Human Rights Watch report documented police abuse. A 2015 BC privacy commissioner report found about 150 emails were removed; in 2018 the RCMP commissioner Brenda Lucki apologized. Police often dismissed missing-person reports, and a 2016 analysis found 'no foul play' labels on cases with unexplained injuries.

segments.title: Missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls
segments.summary: The hosts describe MMIWG as a wider national problem in Canada and the US. Indigenous women and girls are said to be far more likely to go missing or be murdered. Jaime Black's red dress installations led to Canada's Red Dress Day on May 5 since 2010.

segments.title: Inquiry, historical roots and man camps
segments.summary: A national inquiry into MMIWG released a 2019 report on colonial history and exploitation. Reports link man camps for resource extraction work to increased sexual assault of Indigenous women, including in northern British Columbia and North Dakota during its oil boom.

segments.title: Transit and cell coverage efforts
segments.summary: BC Transit launched three bus routes along Highway 16 in 2017, working with Greyhound; Greyhound later cut routes and hitchhiking returned. In 2021 governments funded cell towers with Rogers, with nine of eleven towers up by the end of the previous year.

segments.title: Hopeful billboards and renaming debate
segments.summary: Carrier Sekani Family Services replaced earlier billboards, which used the phrase 'girls don't hitchhike', with messages such as 'We are hope, we are strength.' They proposed renaming the highway the Highway of Hope; critics including Gladys Radek opposed the rename as premature.

segments.title: Listener mail: mushroom fruit
segments.summary: Listener Mike, a mushroom farmer, corrects the Catacombs episode: mushrooms are the fruit, mycelium is the plant, and some supplements use mycelium grain without fruiting bodies.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and note the podcast's production credits.
